claim: Hypothalamic neurons respond to nutritional cues by altering gene expression and neuronal excitability.
source: Hypothalamic neurons respond to nutritional cues by altering gene expression and neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research context.

claim: POMC neurons in mice can be activated or inhibited by insulin.
source: Here we define populations of POMC neurons in mice that are activated or inhibited by insulin and thereby repress or inhibit hepatic glucose production (HGP).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1.

claim: POMC neurons activated or inhibited by insulin can repress or inhibit hepatic glucose production (HGP).
source: Here we define populations of POMC neurons in mice that are activated or inhibited by insulin and thereby repress or inhibit hepatic glucose production (HGP).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance tests and hepatic gene expression data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin is dependent on the regulation of insulin receptor signaling by the phosphatase TCPTP.
source: The proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin was dependent on the regulation of insulin receptor signaling by the phosphatase TCPTP, which is increased by fasting, degraded after feeding and elevated in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in TCPTP-deficient mice and TCPTP inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: TCPTP is increased by fasting.
source: The proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin was dependent on the regulation of insulin receptor signaling by the phosphatase TCPTP, which is increased by fasting, degraded after feeding and elevated in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript (Dodd et al., 2017).

claim: TCPTP is degraded after feeding.
source: The proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin was dependent on the regulation of insulin receptor signaling by the phosphatase TCPTP, which is increased by fasting, degraded after feeding and elevated in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript (Dodd et al., 2017).

claim: TCPTP is elevated in diet-induced obesity.
source: The proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin was dependent on the regulation of insulin receptor signaling by the phosphatase TCPTP, which is increased by fasting, degraded after feeding and elevated in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency enhanced insulin signaling in POMC neurons.
source: TCPTP-deficiency enhanced insulin signaling and the proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin to repress HGP.
evidence: This is supported by p-AKT immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency increased the proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin to repress HGP.
source: TCPTP-deficiency enhanced insulin signaling and the proportion of POMC neurons activated by insulin to repress HGP.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 1 and pyruvate tolerance tests in Figure 3.

claim: Elevated TCPTP in POMC neurons in obesity repressed insulin signaling.
source: Elevated TCPTP in POMC neurons in obesity and/or after fasting repressed insulin signaling, the activation of POMC neurons by insulin and the insulin-induced and POMC-mediated repression of HGP.
evidence: This is supported by p-AKT immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated TCPTP in POMC neurons in obesity repressed the activation of POMC neurons by insulin.
source: Elevated TCPTP in POMC neurons in obesity and/or after fasting repressed insulin signaling, the activation of POMC neurons by insulin and the insulin-induced and POMC-mediated repression of HGP.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice shown in Figure 1.

claim: Elevated TCPTP in POMC neurons in obesity repressed the insulin-induced and POMC-mediated repression of HGP.
source: Elevated TCPTP in POMC neurons in obesity and/or after fasting repressed insulin signaling, the activation of POMC neurons by insulin and the insulin-induced and POMC-mediated repression of HGP.
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance tests and hepatic gene expression data in high-fat fed mice shown in Figure 7.

claim: Insulin acts on peripheral tissues including liver, muscle and adipose tissue to directly control glucose metabolism.
source: Insulin acts on peripheral tissues including liver, muscle and adipose tissue to directly control glucose metabolism, while also acting in the brain to concordantly regulate nutrient fluxes, feeding behaviour and energy homeostasis (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.

claim: Insulin acts in the brain to regulate nutrient fluxes, feeding behaviour and energy homeostasis.
source: Insulin acts on peripheral tissues including liver, muscle and adipose tissue to directly control glucose metabolism, while also acting in the brain to concordantly regulate nutrient fluxes, feeding behaviour and energy homeostasis (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.

claim: The CNS effects of insulin on metabolism are mediated by different brain regions, in particular the hypothalamus.
source: The CNS effects of insulin on metabolism are mediated by different brain regions, in particular the hypothalamus, acting via autonomic circuits to influence peripheral organs, including the pancreas, liver, white adipose tissue and brown adipose tissue to modulate insulin secretion, endogenous glucose production and glucose uptake (Dodd et al., 2015; Könner et al., 2007; Obici et al., 2002b; Pocai et al., 2005; Steculorum et al., 2016; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Vogt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Dodd et al., 2015; Könner et al., 2007; Obici et al., 2002b; Pocai et al., 2005; Steculorum et al., 2016; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Vogt et al., 2014).

claim: The insulin receptor (IR) is widely expressed throughout the brain.
source: The insulin receptor (IR) is widely expressed throughout the brain (Havrankova et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Havrankova et al., 1978.

claim: Mice lacking the IR in the brain exhibit whole-body insulin resistance accompanied by increased food intake and obesity.
source: Mice lacking the IR in the brain exhibit whole-body insulin resistance accompanied by increased food intake and obesity (Brüning et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brüning et al., 2000.

claim: The arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus is a specialized brain region comprising of neurons proximal to the fenestrated capillaries of the median eminence.
source: The contributions of the IR in controlling feeding and energy expenditure are best understood in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus, a specialized brain region comprising of neurons proximal to the fenestrated capillaries of the median eminence.
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical location of the ARC based on established knowledge.

claim: The position of ARC neurons allows them to respond to peripheral circulating factors such as leptin and insulin.
source: This position allows ARC neurons to respond to peripheral circulating factors such as leptin and insulin that convey information on the nutritional and metabolic status of the organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical position of ARC neurons near fenestrated capillaries.

claim: The ARC comprises of proopiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons that suppress appetite.
source: In particular, the ARC comprises of two opposing neuronal populations, the appetite suppressing proopiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons and the orexigenic agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons that co-express neuropeptide Y (NPY) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ARC neuronal populations.

claim: The ARC comprises of orexigenic agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons that co-express neuropeptide Y (NPY) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
source: In particular, the ARC comprises of two opposing neuronal populations, the appetite suppressing proopiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons and the orexigenic agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons that co-express neuropeptide Y (NPY) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ARC neuronal populations.

claim: The activation of POMC neurons results in POMC processing to generate α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH).
source: The activation of POMC neurons results in POMC processing to generate α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), which is released and agonises melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) on neurons in other regions of the brain, such as the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.

claim: α-MSH is released and agonises melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) on neurons in other regions of the brain, such as the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH).
source: The activation of POMC neurons results in POMC processing to generate α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), which is released and agonises melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) on neurons in other regions of the brain, such as the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.

claim: The activation of AgRP/NPY neurons promotes the synthesis and release of AgRP and GABA that antagonise α-MSH/MC4R interactions and directly inhibit POMC neurons.
source: The activation of AgRP/NPY neurons promotes the synthesis and release of AgRP and GABA that antagonise α-MSH/MC4R interactions and directly inhibit POMC neurons, respectively (Atasoy et al., 2012; Cowley et al., 2001; Cowley et al., 2003; Tong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Atasoy et al., 2012; Cowley et al., 2001; Cowley et al., 2003; Tong et al., 2008).

claim: Insulin binds to its tyrosine kinase receptor and signals via the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase PKB/AKT pathway to hyperpolarise and inhibit AgRP/NPY neurons.
source: Insulin binds to its tyrosine kinase receptor and signals via the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase PKB/AKT pathway to hyperpolarise and inhibit AgRP/NPY neurons and repress Agrp expression (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: Insulin represses Agrp expression in AgRP/NPY neurons.
source: Insulin binds to its tyrosine kinase receptor and signals via the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase PKB/AKT pathway to hyperpolarise and inhibit AgRP/NPY neurons and repress Agrp expression (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: Leptin hyperpolarizes and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons and represses Npy/Agrp expression.
source: Leptin also hyperpolarizes and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons and represses Npy/Agrp expression acting via several pathways, including the Janus-activated kinase (JAK)−2/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)−3 pathway and the PI3K/AKT pathway (Cowley et al., 2001; Elias et al., 1999; van den Top et al., 2004; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cowley et al., 2001; Elias et al., 1999; van den Top et al., 2004; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: IR signaling in AgRP neurons is important for the control of peripheral glucose metabolism.
source: IR signaling in AgRP neurons is important for the control of peripheral glucose metabolism (Dodd et al., 2018; Könner et al., 2007) acting through vagal efferents to the liver and α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors to repress hepatic glucose production (HGP) (Kimura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Dodd et al., 2018; Könner et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2016).

claim: Central insulin signaling suppresses HGP by activating Kupffer cells to release interleukin-6 (IL-6).
source: Central insulin signaling suppresses HGP by activating Kupffer cells to release interleukin- 6 (IL-6) (Obici et al., 2002a; Obici et al., 2002b; Pocai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Obici et al., 2002a; Obici et al., 2002b; Pocai et al., 2005).

claim: IL-6 acts on hepatocytes via STAT-3 to repress the expression of gluconeogenic enzymes such as glucose-6-phosphatase (encoded by G6pc).
source: IL-6 in turn acts on hepatocytes via STAT-3 to repress the expression of gluconeogenic enzymes such as glucose-6-phosphatase (encoded by G6pc) (Inoue et al., 2006; Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Inoue et al., 2006; Inoue et al., 2004).

claim: IR deletion in AgRP neurons in mice results in defective inhibition of HGP accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased G6pc hepatic gene expression.
source: IR deletion in AgRP neurons in mice results in defective inhibition of HGP accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased G6pc hepatic gene expression (Könner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Könner et al., 2007.

claim: Leptin depolarises and activates POMC neurons and promotes Pomc expression and α-MSH secretion to repress feeding, increase energy expenditure and repress HGP.
source: Leptin depolarises and activates POMC neurons and promotes Pomc expression and α-MSH secretion to repress feeding, increase energy expenditure and repress HGP (Berglund et al., 2012; Caron et al., 2018; Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Berglund et al., 2012; Caron et al., 2018; Varela and Horvath, 2012).

claim: Insulin has been traditionally viewed as an inhibitor of POMC neuronal excitation, hyperpolarising POMC neurons through the engagement of ATP-sensitive K+ channels.
source: By contrast insulin has been traditionally viewed as an inhibitor of POMC neuronal excitation, hyperpolarising POMC neurons through the engagement of ATP-sensitive K+ channels (Hill et al., 2008; Könner et al., 2007; Plum et al., 2006; Spanswick et al., 2000; Williams et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Hill et al., 2008; Könner et al., 2007; Plum et al., 2006; Spanswick et al., 2000; Williams et al., 2010).

claim: Insulin can depolarise and activate POMC neurons via the activation of transient receptor potential (TRPC)−5 channels.
source: More recent studies have shown that insulin can depolarise and activate POMC neurons via the activation of transient receptor potential (TRPC)−5 channels (Qiu et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2014), whereas several studies have shown that insulin can promote Pomc expression and the melanocortin response (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Qiu et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2014).

claim: Insulin can promote Pomc expression and the melanocortin response.
source: More recent studies have shown that insulin can depolarise and activate POMC neurons via the activation of transient receptor potential (TRPC)−5 channels (Qiu et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2014), whereas several studies have shown that insulin can promote Pomc expression and the melanocortin response (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomics has led to the identification of different subsets of POMC- and AgRP-expressing neurons that exhibit distinct transcriptional responses to changing energy status.
source: The advent of single-cell transcriptomics has yielded unprecedented insight into the heterogeneity of hypothalamic cell types and has led to the identification of different subsets of POMC- and AgRP-expressing neurons that exhibit distinct transcriptional responses to changing energy status (Campbell et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Henry et al., 2015; Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Campbell et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Henry et al., 2015; Lam et al., 2017).

claim: IR deletion in POMC neurons does not influence glucose metabolism.
source: Irrespective, whereas insulin signaling in AgRP neurons overtly affects glucose metabolism through the control of HGP and brown adipose tissue glucose uptake (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017), gene deletion and pharmacogenetic experiments have suggested that insulin signaling in POMC neurons may not be so important; neither IR deletion in POMC neurons (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017) nor the acute activation of POMC neurons using DREADDs (Steculorum et al., 2016) influences glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017).

claim: The acute activation of POMC neurons using DREADDs does not influence glucose metabolism.
source: Irrespective, whereas insulin signaling in AgRP neurons overtly affects glucose metabolism through the control of HGP and brown adipose tissue glucose uptake (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017), gene deletion and pharmacogenetic experiments have suggested that insulin signaling in POMC neurons may not be so important; neither IR deletion in POMC neurons (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017) nor the acute activation of POMC neurons using DREADDs (Steculorum et al., 2016) influences glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Steculorum et al., 2016.

claim: The combined deletion of the IR plus leptin receptor in POMC neurons profoundly affects glucose homeostasis and results in systemic insulin resistance and increased HGP.
source: Nonetheless, the combined deletion of the IR plus leptin receptor in POMC neurons profoundly affects glucose homeostasis and results in systemic insulin resistance and increased HGP (Hill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2010.

claim: TCPTP is an IR phosphatase whose abundance in the ARC is increased by fasting and repressed by feeding.
source: We report that insulin can elicit discordant effects on the electrophysiological activity of POMC neurons and that this is regulated by T-cell protein tyrosine phosphatase (TCPTP) (Tiganis, 2013), an IR phosphatase whose abundance in the ARC is increased by fasting and repressed by feeding (Dodd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Tiganis, 2013; Dodd et al., 2017).

claim: The majority of POMC neurons from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP reporter mice were either inhibited by insulin (27/53, 50.9%) or were unaffected by insulin (20/53, 37.7%).
source: The majority of POMC neurons were either inhibited by insulin (27/53, 50.9%) with a significant membrane hyperpolarisation (baseline −42.5 ± 1.2 mV; insulin −45.9 ± 1.8 mV) and decreased firing rate (baseline 1.09 ± 0.20 Hz; insulin 0.2 ± 0.06 Hz) or were unaffected by insulin (20/53, 37.7%) with minimal changes in membrane potential (baseline −46.8 ± 1.7 mV; insulin −45.7 ± 1.8 mV) and non-significant changes in firing rate (baseline 1.32 ± 0.51 Hz; insulin 1.08 ± 0.41 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: A smaller subset of POMC neurons (6/53, 11.3%) from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP reporter mice were activated by insulin.
source: A smaller subset of POMC neurons (6/53, 11.3%) were activated by insulin exhibiting significant membrane depolarisation (baseline −45.9 ± 2.4 mV; insulin −40.1 ± 2.5 mV) and increased firing rates (baseline 0.99 ± 0.37 Hz; insulin 1.69 ± 0.60 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: Insulin-inhibited POMC neurons exhibited significant membrane hyperpolarisation (baseline −42.5 ± 1.2 mV; insulin −45.9 ± 1.8 mV) and decreased firing rate (baseline 1.09 ± 0.20 Hz; insulin 0.2 ± 0.06 Hz).
source: The majority of POMC neurons were either inhibited by insulin (27/53, 50.9%) with a significant membrane hyperpolarisation (baseline −42.5 ± 1.2 mV; insulin −45.9 ± 1.8 mV) and decreased firing rate (baseline 1.09 ± 0.20 Hz; insulin 0.2 ± 0.06 Hz) or were unaffected by insulin (20/53, 37.7%) with minimal changes in membrane potential (baseline −46.8 ± 1.7 mV; insulin −45.7 ± 1.8 mV) and non-significant changes in firing rate (baseline 1.32 ± 0.51 Hz; insulin 1.08 ± 0.41 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: Insulin-activated POMC neurons exhibited significant membrane depolarisation (baseline −45.9 ± 2.4 mV; insulin −40.1 ± 2.5 mV) and increased firing rates (baseline 0.99 ± 0.37 Hz; insulin 1.69 ± 0.60 Hz).
source: A smaller subset of POMC neurons (6/53, 11.3%) were activated by insulin exhibiting significant membrane depolarisation (baseline −45.9 ± 2.4 mV; insulin −40.1 ± 2.5 mV) and increased firing rates (baseline 0.99 ± 0.37 Hz; insulin 1.69 ± 0.60 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: Excited POMC neurons were located more medially and comparatively closer to the third ventricle.
source: Although the unresponsive and inhibited POMC neurons did not exhibit any distinct anatomical distribution, the excited POMC neurons were located more medially and comparatively closer to the third ventricle. (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the camera lucida image in Figure 1d showing the topographical localization of insulin-responsive POMC neuronal subtypes.

claim: The majority of inhibited (25/27) and around half of all unresponsive (11/20) POMC neurons in patch-clamped coronal slices from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP mice expressed TCPTP.
source: We found that the majority of inhibited (25/27) and around half of all unresponsive (11/20) POMC neurons in the patch-clamped coronal slices from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP mice expressed TCPTP (Figure 1e–f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1e-f.

claim: Most (5/6) of POMC neurons that were excited by insulin did not express TCPTP.
source: On the other hand, most (5/6) of POMC neurons that were excited by insulin did not express TCPTP (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency significantly increased the number of POMC neurons that were excited (12/33, 36.4%) in response to insulin.
source: Strikingly TCPTP-deficiency significantly increased the number of cells that were excited (12/33, 36.4%) in response to insulin and decreased the number of inhibited (12/33, 36.4%) POMC neurons; TCPTP-deficiency tended to decrease the number of unresponsive (9/33, 27.3%) POMC neurons but this was not significant (Figure 1g–h; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in POMC-TC mice shown in Figure 1g-h.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency decreased the number of inhibited (12/33, 36.4%) POMC neurons.
source: Strikingly TCPTP-deficiency significantly increased the number of cells that were excited (12/33, 36.4%) in response to insulin and decreased the number of inhibited (12/33, 36.4%) POMC neurons; TCPTP-deficiency tended to decrease the number of unresponsive (9/33, 27.3%) POMC neurons but this was not significant (Figure 1g–h; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in POMC-TC mice shown in Figure 1g-h.

claim: TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons activated by insulin increased to 33% (19/58 cells).
source: Strikingly, TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons activated by insulin increased to 33% (19/58 cells) (Figure 1i; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Pomc-eGFP mice treated with TCPTP inhibitor shown in Figure 1i.

claim: In high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons inhibited by insulin increased from 51% (27/53 cells) to 65% (22/34 cells).
source: Consistent with this, we found that in high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons inhibited by insulin ex vivo increased from 51% (27/53 cells) to 65% (22/34 cells; p=0.045; Supplementary file 2), whereas the proportion of cells being activated fell from 11% (6/53 cells) to 3% (1/34 cells; p=0.027, Figure 1k; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice shown in Figure 1k.

claim: In high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of POMC neurons being activated by insulin fell from 11% (6/53 cells) to 3% (1/34 cells).
source: Consistent with this, we found that in high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons inhibited by insulin ex vivo increased from 51% (27/53 cells) to 65% (22/34 cells; p=0.045; Supplementary file 2), whereas the proportion of cells being activated fell from 11% (6/53 cells) to 3% (1/34 cells; p=0.027, Figure 1k; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice shown in Figure 1k.

claim: TCPTP inhibition in high-fat-fed mice significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that only 20% (7/35 cells) of GFP-positive POMC neurons were inhibited by insulin.
source: Strikingly, TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that only 20% (7/35 cells) of GFP-positive POMC neurons were inhibited by insulin, whereas the proportion of cells being activated increased from 3% (1/34 cells) to 37% (13/35; p<0.001, Figure 1k–l; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice treated with TCPTP inhibitor shown in Figure 1k-l.

claim: TCPTP inhibition in high-fat-fed mice increased the proportion of POMC neurons being activated by insulin from 3% (1/34 cells) to 37% (13/35).
source: Strikingly, TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that only 20% (7/35 cells) of GFP-positive POMC neurons were inhibited by insulin, whereas the proportion of cells being activated increased from 3% (1/34 cells) to 37% (13/35; p<0.001, Figure 1k–l; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice treated with TCPTP inhibitor shown in Figure 1k-l.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC-TC mice increased c-Fos staining in the PVH of fasted mice and this was exacerbated by insulin.
source: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC-TC mice increased c-Fos staining (a surrogate marker of neuronal activation) in the PVH of fasted mice and this was exacerbated by insulin (Figure 1m); although systemic insulin administration resulted in hypoglycemia, this was similar in Ptpn2fl/fl and POMC-TC mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1m.

claim: The acute inhibition of POMC neurons had no effect on HGP.
source: We found that the acute inhibition of POMC neurons had no effect, whereas the inhibition of POMC neurons over 6 hr increased blood glucose levels in response to pyruvate, consistent with the promotion of HGP (Figure 2c); CNO had no effect on the electrophysiological response of non-DREADD expressing POMC neurons (data not shown) and did not alter glucose metabolism (as assessed by measuring glucose excursions in response to pyruvate, glucose or insulin) in C57BL/6 control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The inhibition of POMC neurons over 6 hr increased blood glucose levels in response to pyruvate, consistent with the promotion of HGP.
source: We found that the acute inhibition of POMC neurons had no effect, whereas the inhibition of POMC neurons over 6 hr increased blood glucose levels in response to pyruvate, consistent with the promotion of HGP (Figure 2c); CNO had no effect on the electrophysiological response of non-DREADD expressing POMC neurons (data not shown) and did not alter glucose metabolism (as assessed by measuring glucose excursions in response to pyruvate, glucose or insulin) in C57BL/6 control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The chronic, but not acute inhibition of POMC neurons was accompanied by the significant repression of hepatic Il6 expression and diminished hepatic STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation.
source: We found that the chronic, but not acute inhibition of POMC neurons was accompanied by the significant repression of hepatic Il6 expression and diminished hepatic STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation (Figure 2d–e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and qPCR data shown in Figure 2d-e.

claim: Chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with increased expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc.
source: This in turn was associated with increased expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with attenuated insulin-mediated repression of endogenous glucose production.
source: We found that chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with attenuated insulin-mediated repression of endogenous glucose production and an overall decrease in insulin sensitivity as assessed by the reduced glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia during the clamp and the reduced glucose disappearance rate (Rd; Figure 2f–g; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2f-g.

claim: Chronic POMC neuronal inhibition resulted in an overall decrease in insulin sensitivity as assessed by the reduced glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia during the clamp and the reduced glucose disappearance rate (Rd).
source: We found that chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with attenuated insulin-mediated repression of endogenous glucose production and an overall decrease in insulin sensitivity as assessed by the reduced glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia during the clamp and the reduced glucose disappearance rate (Rd; Figure 2f–g; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2f-g.

claim: The attenuated repression of endogenous glucose production by chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression.
source: The attenuated repression of endogenous glucose production was accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 2h), in keeping with the attenuated repression of HGP.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Chronic POMC neuronal activation resulted in the suppression of glucose excursion in response to pyruvate in keeping with the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis.
source: Chronic but not acute POMC neuronal activation resulted in the suppression of glucose excursion in response to pyruvate (Figure 2j) in keeping with the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and was accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation and the significant repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 2k–l).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Chronic POMC neuronal activation was accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation and the significant repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression.
source: Chronic but not acute POMC neuronal activation resulted in the suppression of glucose excursion in response to pyruvate (Figure 2j) in keeping with the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and was accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation and the significant repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 2k–l).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and qPCR data shown in Figure 2k-l.

claim: TCPTP deletion in POMC neurons resulted in improved pyruvate tolerance at doses of insulin that elicited little to no effect in Ptpn2fl/fl control mice.
source: At doses of insulin that elicited little to no effect in Ptpn2fl/fl control mice, we found that TCPTP deletion in POMC neurons resulted in improved pyruvate tolerance, as assessed by the suppression of pyruvate-induced increases in blood glucose levels (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The improved pyruvate tolerance in POMC-TC mice was accompanied by increased ICV insulin-induced hypothalamic Pomc and hepatic Il6 gene expression as well as increased hepatic p-STAT-3.
source: The improved pyruvate tolerance was accompanied by increased ICV insulin-induced hypothalamic Pomc and hepatic Il6 gene expression as well as increased hepatic p-STAT-3 (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3c-e.

claim: The hepatic expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc expression was elevated in overnight fasted POMC-TC mice.
source: The hepatic expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc expression was elevated in overnight fasted POMC-TC mice (Figure 3d), probably as a compensatory mechanism to prevent hypoglycemia.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The increased hepatic STAT3 signaling in ICV insulin-administered POMC-TC mice was associated with the increased repression of hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression.
source: Nonetheless the increased hepatic STAT3 signaling in ICV insulin-administered POMC-TC mice was associated with the increased repression of hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons was accompanied by lower fasted (6 hr) blood glucose and plasma insulin levels.
source: TCPTP-deficiency was accompanied by lower fasted (6 hr) blood glucose and plasma insulin levels, in keeping with overall improvements in glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose and plasma insulin measurements shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons resulted in greater reductions in blood glucose levels in response to insulin and improved glucose clearances in response to a bolus of glucose.
source: This was reflected in greater reductions in blood glucose levels in response to insulin and improved glucose clearances in response to a bolus of glucose (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by insulin and glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Excursions in blood glucose in response to pyruvate were attenuated in POMC-TC mice in keeping with reduced endogenous glucose production.
source: Moreover, excursions in blood glucose in response to pyruvate were attenuated in keeping with reduced endogenous glucose production (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice, consistent with enhanced whole-body insulin sensitivity.
source: We found that the glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice, consistent with enhanced whole-body insulin sensitivity (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The glucose disappearance rate (Rd) was unaltered by TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons under the conditions tested.
source: Importantly we found that the glucose disappearance rate (Rd), which primarily measures muscle and adipose tissue glucose uptake, was unaltered by TCPTP-deficiency under the conditions tested, whereas the insulin-induced repression of endogenous glucose production, a measure of hepatic and renal glucose production, was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice (Figure 4f; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The insulin-induced repression of endogenous glucose production was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice.
source: Importantly we found that the glucose disappearance rate (Rd), which primarily measures muscle and adipose tissue glucose uptake, was unaltered by TCPTP-deficiency under the conditions tested, whereas the insulin-induced repression of endogenous glucose production, a measure of hepatic and renal glucose production, was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice (Figure 4f; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The repressed endogenous glucose production in POMC-TC mice was accompanied by decreased expression of hepatic gluconeogenic genes (Pck1 and G6pc).
source: The repressed endogenous glucose production was accompanied by decreased expression of hepatic gluconeogenic genes (Pck1 and G6pc, Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Insulin-induced IR Y1162/Y1163 tyrosine phosphorylation and activation and downstream PI3K/AKT signaling in the liver were dramatically enhanced by POMC TCPTP deficiency.
source: In keeping with the overall improvement in insulin sensitivity we found that insulin-induced IR Y1162/Y1163 tyrosine phosphorylation and activation and downstream PI3K/AKT signaling in the liver (as monitored by AKT Ser-473 phosphorylation) were dramatically enhanced by POMC TCPTP deficiency (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Insulin-induced PI3K/Akt signaling was not altered in skeletal muscle or white adipose tissue by POMC TCPTP deficiency.
source: By contrast insulin-induced PI3K/Akt signaling was not altered in skeletal muscle or white adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: In fed mice, ICV administered insulin repressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as assessed by the attenuated glucose excursions in response to pyruvate and the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene expression (Pck1 and G6pc).
source: We found that in fed mice, ICV administered insulin repressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as assessed by the attenuated glucose excursions in response to pyruvate (Figure 5b) and the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene expression (Pck1 and G6pc; Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test and qPCR data shown in Figure 5b-c.

claim: ICV insulin in fed mice was accompanied by the promotion of hepatic Il6 expression.
source: This was accompanied by the promotion of hepatic Il6 expression (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In food-restricted mice, ICV administered insulin had no effect on pyruvate-induced glucose excursions or the expression of Pck1, G6pc and Il6.
source: By contrast, in food-restricted mice (Figure 5d), ICV administered insulin had no effect on pyruvate-induced glucose excursions (Figure 5e) or the expression of Pck1, G6pc and Il6 (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test and qPCR data shown in Figure 5e-f.

claim: ICV insulin had no effect on glucose excursions in response to pyruvate in food-restricted Ptpn2fl/fl mice.
source: As in food-restricted C57BL/6 mice, ICV insulin had no effect on glucose excursions in response to pyruvate in food-restricted Ptpn2fl/fl mice (Figure 5g), nor did it alter the expression of Pck1, G6pc or Il6 (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test and qPCR data shown in Figure 5g-h.

claim: Glucose excursions in vehicle-treated POMC-TC mice were reduced relative to Ptpn2fl/fl mice and reduced further in response to ICV insulin administration.
source: By contrast glucose excursions in vehicle-treated POMC-TC mice were reduced relative to Ptpn2fl/fl mice and reduced further in response to ICV insulin administration (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: ICV administered insulin dramatically reduced hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression below that in Ptpn2fl/fl controls in food-restricted POMC-TC mice and was accompanied by a greater than two-fold increase in Il6 expression.
source: Nonetheless, ICV administered insulin dramatically reduced hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression below that in Ptpn2fl/fl controls and was accompanied by a greater than two-fold increase in Il6 expression (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: TCPTP deficiency enhanced insulin-induced ARC PI3K/AKT signaling in POMC neurons.
source: Consistent with our previous studies (Dodd et al., 2015) we found that TCPTP deficiency enhanced insulin-induced ARC PI3K/AKT signaling in POMC neurons, as assessed by monitoring for AKT Ser-473 phosphorylation (p-AKT) in mice on the Pomc-eGFP reporter background.
evidence: This is supported by p-AKT immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a-b and citations (Dodd et al., 2015).

claim: The enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling otherwise associated with TCPTP-deficiency was significantly repressed, albeit not completely corrected by IR heterozygosity.
source: Importantly, we found that the enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling otherwise associated with TCPTP-deficiency was significantly repressed, albeit not completely corrected by IR heterozygosity (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is supported by p-AKT immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: IR heterozygosity significantly decreased the number of POMC neurons that were activated by insulin in POMC-TC mice, from 36% (12/33) to 17% (8/48).
source: IR heterozygosity significantly decreased the number of POMC neurons that were activated by insulin in POMC-TC mice, from 36% (12/33; Figure 1g; Supplementary file 1) to 17% (8/48; Figure 6c), so that the proportion of activated neurons in POMC-TC-IR mice was not significantly different from controls (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Hypothalamic Pomc gene expression and α-MSH staining in the PVH were increased in POMC-TC mice and these were corrected by IR heterozygosity.
source: We found that hypothalamic Pomc gene expression (Figure 6e) and α-MSH staining in the PVH were increased in POMC-TC mice and these were corrected by IR heterozygosity (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: The enhanced insulin-POMC-mediated repression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and improved glucose metabolism in POMC-TC mice were largely corrected in POMC-TC-IR mice.
source: Moreover, we found that the enhanced insulin-POMC-mediated repression of hepatic gluconeogenesis (as assessed by the ability of ICV insulin to repress pyruvate-induced glucose excursions and hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression; Figure 6g–i) and improved glucose metabolism (as assessed in glucose, insulin and pyruvate tolerance tests and by measuring blood glucose levels; Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–d) in POMC-TC mice were largely corrected in POMC-TC-IR mice so that POMC-TC-IR mice more closely resembled Ptpn2fl/fl controls; ICV insulin did not affect body weight, food intake or adiposity in Ptpn2fl/fl, POMC-TC or POMC-TC-IR mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test, qPCR, glucose tolerance test, insulin tolerance test, and blood glucose measurement data shown in Figure 6g-i and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a-d.

claim: TCPTP deficiency in POMC neurons repressed pyruvate-induced glucose excursions in response to ICV insulin in obese mice.
source: Whereas control mice remained unresponsive to ICV insulin, TCPTP deficiency in POMC neurons repressed pyruvate-induced glucose excursions in response to ICV insulin and this was accompanied by increased hepatic Il6 expression and STAT-3 signaling and the repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 7a–d).
evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test, qPCR, and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7a-d.

claim: TCPTP deficiency in POMC neurons in obese mice was accompanied by increased hepatic Il6 expression and STAT-3 signaling and the repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression in response to ICV insulin.
source: Whereas control mice remained unresponsive to ICV insulin, TCPTP deficiency in POMC neurons repressed pyruvate-induced glucose excursions in response to ICV insulin and this was accompanied by increased hepatic Il6 expression and STAT-3 signaling and the repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 7a–d).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: Blood glucose and plasma insulin levels in 12 hr fasted POMC-TC mice on high fat diet were reduced, consistent with improved whole-body insulin sensitivity.
source: However, blood glucose and plasma insulin levels in 12 hr fasted mice were reduced, consistent with improved whole-body insulin sensitivity (Figure 7e–f).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose and plasma insulin measurements shown in Figure 7e-f.

claim: Glucose infusion rates were significantly increased in POMC-TC mice on high fat diet, consistent with enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity.
source: Glucose infusion rates were significantly increased in POMC-TC mice (Figure 7g; Figure 7—figure supplement 1e), consistent with enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Glucose disappearance (Rd) was unaltered in POMC-TC mice on high fat diet.
source: Although glucose disappearance (Rd) was unaltered (Figure 7h), endogenous glucose production was suppressed in POMC-TC mice (Figure 7i) and accompanied by reduced hepatic gluconeogenic (Pck1 and G6pc) gene expression (Figure 7j).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 7h.

claim: Endogenous glucose production was suppressed in POMC-TC mice on high fat diet and accompanied by reduced hepatic gluconeogenic (Pck1 and G6pc) gene expression.
source: Although glucose disappearance (Rd) was unaltered (Figure 7h), endogenous glucose production was suppressed in POMC-TC mice (Figure 7i) and accompanied by reduced hepatic gluconeogenic (Pck1 and G6pc) gene expression (Figure 7j).
evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data and qPCR shown in Figure 7i-j.

claim: TCPTP protein levels in mediobasal hypothalamic homogenates from fed mice that had been administered a high fat diet for 12 weeks were increased by 6.3 ± 0.49 fold when compared to those in corresponding chow-fed lean controls.
source: Consistent with this, TCPTP protein levels, as assessed by immunoblotting mediobasal hypothalamic homogenates from fed [allowed to feed for 4 hr after start of dark cycle till satiated (Dodd et al., 2017)] mice that had been administered a high fat diet for 12 weeks, were increased by 6.3 ± 0.49 fold when compared to those in corresponding chow-fed lean controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: The increase in TCPTP in high fat diet occurred in hypothalamic neurons of the ARC, including POMC neurons.
source: Importantly, the increase in TCPTP occurred in hypothalamic neurons of the ARC, including POMC neurons, as assessed by the increased coincidence of TCPTP with GFP-positive POMC neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and was accompanied by the repression of insulin-induced PI3K/AKT signaling that was restored by TCPTP-deficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The increase in TCPTP in high fat diet was accompanied by the repression of insulin-induced PI3K/AKT signaling that was restored by TCPTP-deficiency.
source: Importantly, the increase in TCPTP occurred in hypothalamic neurons of the ARC, including POMC neurons, as assessed by the increased coincidence of TCPTP with GFP-positive POMC neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and was accompanied by the repression of insulin-induced PI3K/AKT signaling that was restored by TCPTP-deficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The Pomc-Cre transgene can delete in roughly 25% of NPY/AgRP neurons in early development.
source: Given that the Pomc-Cre transgene can delete in roughly 25% of NPY/AgRP neurons in early development (Padilla et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2018), we cannot exclude that a proportion of the inhibited neurons were in fact AgRP neurons that are inhibited by insulin (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Padilla et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2018).

claim: Feeding-induced repression of hypothalamic TCPTP expression is defective in obesity resulting in elevated TCPTP.
source: We have reported previously that hypothalamic TCPTP levels are elevated in diet-induced obesity (Loh et al., 2011), whereas more recently we have shown that feeding-induced repression of hypothalamic TCPTP expression is defective in obesity resulting in elevated TCPTP (Dodd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Loh et al., 2011; Dodd et al., 2017).

claim: Increases in circulating corticosterone that accompany fasting drive hypothalamic TCPTP expression.
source: Increases in circulating corticosterone that accompany fasting drive hypothalamic TCPTP expression (Dodd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dodd et al., 2017.

claim: Feeding inhibits TCPTP expression and promotes its rapid degradation via the proteasome.
source: By contrast, feeding inhibits TCPTP expression and promotes its rapid degradation via the proteasome (Dodd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dodd et al., 2017.

claim: In AgRP neurons, TCPTP fluxes serve to coordinate the browning and thermogenic activity of white fat with the expenditure of energy linked to feeding.
source: We have reported that in AgRP neurons this serves to coordinate the browning and thermogenic activity of white fat with the expenditure of energy linked to feeding (Dodd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dodd et al., 2017.

claim: Fluxes in TCPTP in AgRP neurons influence hepatic glucose metabolism.
source: In other studies we have shown that such fluxes in TCPTP in AgRP neurons also influence hepatic glucose metabolism (Dodd et al., 2018), which is in keeping with the previously established role for the IR in AgRP neurons in glucose metabolism (Könner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Dodd et al., 2018; Könner et al., 2007).

claim: In cardiomyocytes, insulin-induced PI3K signaling promotes mitochondrial fusion.
source: In cardiomyocytes, insulin-induced PI3K signaling promotes mitochondrial fusion (Parra et al., 2014), but it remains to be established if insulin similarly alters mitochondrial dynamics in POMC neurons and whether TCPTP influences POMC neuron electrophysiologial responses through the IR-mediated control of mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parra et al., 2014.

claim: In humans, peripheral insulin resistance in obesity has been linked to CNS insulin resistance.
source: In humans, peripheral insulin resistance in obesity has been linked to CNS insulin resistance (Anthony et al., 2006; Hirvonen et al., 2011; Tschritter et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Anthony et al., 2006; Hirvonen et al., 2011; Tschritter et al., 2006).

claim: The ability of intranasally administered insulin to elicit effects in the hypothalamus and suppress HGP and promote glucose uptake in lean individuals is defective in overweight individuals.
source: Moreover the ability of intranasally administered insulin to elicit effects in the hypothalamus and suppress HGP and promote glucose uptake in lean individuals is defective in overweight individuals (Heni et al., 2017; Heni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Heni et al., 2017; Heni et al., 2014).

claim: Mitochondrial fusion in AgRP neurons drives ATP production and excitation.
source: Yet another mechanism could involve TCPTP altering mitochondrial dynamics, as mitochondrial fusion in AgRP neurons drives ATP production and excitation (Dietrich et al., 2013; Nasrallah and Horvath, 2014), whereas mitochondrial fusion in POMC neurons drives α-MSH production and the melanocortin response (Schneeberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Dietrich et al., 2013; Nasrallah and Horvath, 2014).

claim: Mitochondrial fusion in POMC neurons drives α-MSH production and the melanocortin response.
source: Yet another mechanism could involve TCPTP altering mitochondrial dynamics, as mitochondrial fusion in AgRP neurons drives ATP production and excitation (Dietrich et al., 2013; Nasrallah and Horvath, 2014), whereas mitochondrial fusion in POMC neurons drives α-MSH production and the melanocortin response (Schneeberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schneeberger et al., 2013.

claim: The GFP reporter faithfully marks POMC neurons in adult mice.
source: We explored the insulin-induced activation of GFP-positive ARC POMC neurons in coronal slices from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP reporter mice using the whole-cell patch clamp technique; previous studies have confirmed that the GFP reporter faithfully marks POMC neurons in adult mice (Padilla et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Padilla et al., 2010.

claim: Cre-dependent AVV expression in the ARC of adult Pomc-Cre mice occurs specifically in POMC neurons.
source: This is also consistent with studies showing that Cre-dependent AVV expression in the ARC of adult Pomc-Cre mice occurs specifically in POMC neurons (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: POMC neuronal activation is accompanied by increased Pomc expression and the processing of POMC to α-MSH.
source: POMC neuronal activation is accompanied by increased Pomc expression and the processing of POMC to α-MSH (Schneeberger et al., 2013); α-MSH is released from POMC neuronal terminals at the PVH where it drives melanocortin-dependent responses (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Schneeberger et al., 2013; Varela and Horvath, 2012).

claim: α-MSH is released from POMC neuronal terminals at the PVH where it drives melanocortin-dependent responses.
source: POMC neuronal activation is accompanied by increased Pomc expression and the processing of POMC to α-MSH (Schneeberger et al., 2013); α-MSH is released from POMC neuronal terminals at the PVH where it drives melanocortin-dependent responses (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.
